messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Media Manager
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 48

Amir is a 56-year-old married man who works as a social media manager for a mid-sized nonprofit. He grew up in the Middle East and immigrated to the United States in his twenties. He describes himself as someone who “used to love people” and who built his career around connection. Now, he says, he feels like a ghost inside his own life.

The traumatic event happened fourteen months ago. Amir was driving home from a late shift, around 11 PM, on a quiet residential street in his city. He had just finished monitoring a heated comment thread on one of the organization’s campaigns. As he approached a stop sign, a police cruiser pulled up behind him and activated its lights. Amir says he felt a familiar knot in his stomach—the kind he learned to live with as a young man in his country of origin. He pulled over immediately, hands on the wheel. The officer approached, flashlight in hand, and asked for his license and registration. Amir reached slowly for the glove compartment. Before he could open it, another officer ran up and yanked open his door. The next few minutes are fragmented in Amir’s memory: shouting, the cold pavement on his face, a knee pressing into his lower back. He was handcuffed, then released after twenty minutes with no charge. The officers told him they had mistaken his car for one reported stolen. They did not apologize.

Amir did not tell his wife about the incident. He went home, showered, and went to bed. The next morning, he looked at himself in the mirror and saw a stranger. For weeks, he convinced himself it was simply a bad night. But then the images started intruding. He would be writing a caption for a post—something about community resilience—and suddenly the white fluorescence of the police lights would flash behind his eyes. He would hear a siren outside his office window and his chest would tighten, his hands gripping the edge of his desk. He began to avoid driving after dark, even though it meant leaving work early or asking colleagues for rides. He told himself it was traffic.

At work, his performance has declined. Amir used to enjoy curating uplifting content, engaging with followers, brainstorming viral campaigns. Now he finds himself hypervigilant about comments—especially any that mention law enforcement or safety. He has started flagging perfectly benign posts for review, afraid they might trigger something. His supervisor has noticed. He spends more time in the restroom, splashing water on his face, trying to slow his breathing. He cannot stand the sound of a zipper because it reminds him of the handcuffs being tightened.

At home, he has grown irritable. His wife, Lina, tries to ask about his day and he snaps, then feels ashamed. He has stopped sleeping in their bed, preferring the couch because the bedroom window faces the street and every pair of headlights makes him freeze. He replays the event in his mind, trying to understand what he did wrong. He blames himself for pulling over too slowly, for reaching toward the glove compartment, for being the kind of person whose car is mistaken for stolen.

Lina found him one night staring at a blank screen, his hands trembling. She asked what was wrong, and for the first time, he told her. He said the words as if they were a confession. She held him, but he could not feel her. He now avoids the street where it happened, even if it adds twenty minutes to his commute. He avoids the police station in his neighborhood. He avoids the color of the police uniform—a dark blue that used to mean nothing and now feels like a warning.

Amir’s PCL-5 score is 48. He still shows up to work. He still comes home. But he describes himself as living behind a glass wall, watching the world move without him.
